Using the WPL batting styles app

Source: vignettes/using-the-app.Rmd
using-the-app.Rmd

Who this package is for

a4 helps a WPL franchise analyst preparing for the player auction answer one question:

In a given season, which batters score quickly without wasting balls, and how do they compare with the rest of the league?

The package contains:

  • wpl_batters: season-level batting summaries for every Women’s Premier League batter who faced at least 20 balls in a season;
  • batting_profile(): a function that compares batters with the league median for a season and labels their scoring style; and
  • run_app(): an interactive Shiny app built on the two above.

Installation

Install the package from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-vnay0004")

Then load it:

library(a4)

Launching the app 

run_app()

The app opens in your browser or in your IDE’s viewer.

Using the controls

Control What it does
Season Chooses which WPL season to analyse. Cricsheet labels seasons like 2024/25; that season was played in early 2025.
Team Shows only one franchise’s batters. They are still compared with the whole league’s medians.
Minimum balls faced Excludes batters with small samples. Raise it when you want only established batters.

A suggested workflow for an analyst:

  1. Choose the most recent season and leave Team on All teams.
  2. Set Minimum balls faced to about 100 to focus on regular batters.
  3. Look in the upper-left of the chart for attacking batters.
  4. Switch to an earlier season to see whether those batters were consistent.
  5. Select your own franchise to see where your current batters sit.

Reading the outputs

The scatter plot places each batter by dot-ball percentage (horizontal) and boundary percentage (vertical). The dashed lines are the league medians for the season, which split the chart into four styles:

Region Style Meaning
Upper-left Attacking More boundaries, fewer dot balls than the median
Lower-left Rotator Few boundaries, but keeps the strike moving
Upper-right Boundary-reliant Hits boundaries but faces many dots
Lower-right Low tempo Few boundaries and many dots

Larger points faced more balls, so their percentages are more reliable. The five leading run-scorers are labelled.

The value boxes summarise the current selection: how many batters qualify, who scored most runs, and how many are attacking.

The table lists the ten leading run-scorers in the selection with their rates and style.

The same analysis without the app

batting_profile() performs the calculation behind the app, so you can reproduce any view in your own code:

profile_2025 <- batting_profile(wpl_batters, "2024/25", min_balls = 100)
head(profile_2025[, c("batter", "batting_team", "runs",
                      "dot_percent", "boundary_percent", "style")])
## # A tibble: 6 × 6
##   batter          batting_team           runs dot_percent boundary_percent style
##   <chr>           <chr>                 <int>       <dbl>            <dbl> <chr>
## 1 NR Sciver-Brunt Mumbai Indians          523        30               25.7 Atta…
## 2 EA Perry        Royal Challengers Be…   372        29.6             20.4 Atta…
## 3 HK Matthews     Mumbai Indians          307        48               20.4 Boun…
## 4 Shafali Verma   Delhi Capitals          304        42.7             25.1 Boun…
## 5 H Kaur          Mumbai Indians          302        36.4             25.1 Atta…
## 6 MM Lanning      Delhi Capitals          276        45.3             19.8 Low …

How many qualifying batters fall into each style?

table(profile_2025$style)
## 
##        Attacking Boundary-reliant        Low tempo          Rotator 
##                5                4                5                3

Which batters were attacking?

profile_2025$batter[profile_2025$style == "Attacking"]
## [1] "NR Sciver-Brunt" "EA Perry"        "H Kaur"          "A Gardner"      
## [5] "RM Ghosh"

Interpreting a finding

✏️ Write 2–4 sentences in your own words about something you noticed in the app. For example: which batter stood out in a season, whether attacking batters were also the top run-scorers, or whether a player’s style changed between seasons. Refer to the numbers above.

Limitations

✏️ Write 2–3 sentences in your own words. Points worth considering:

  • the rates ignore batting position: openers face the new ball and powerplay fields, while finishers bat at the death;
  • they ignore match situation and opposition strength;
  • styles are relative to the season median, so “Low tempo” is not the same as “poor”;
  • batters close to a dashed line could easily switch style with a few balls’ difference.

Data source

Data come from Cricsheet, accessed through the cricketdata package, and are used under the Open Data Commons Attribution License (ODC-BY 1.0). The preparation script is data-raw/wpl_batters.R in the package repository.
